messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 58
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Forensic Analyst
- Trauma Type: Man-made disaster
- Pcl5: 43

# The Weight of Evidence

Roberto is a 58-year-old Colombian-born forensic analyst who has spent more than three decades making sense of chaos — cataloguing, measuring, and documenting the aftermath of violence so that courts and investigators can find meaning in what remains. He is methodical by nature, a man who has always found comfort in procedure. His colleagues describe him as unshakeable. His wife, Marisol, uses the same word, though lately she says it with less certainty.

Fourteen months ago, Roberto was part of a specialized response team deployed to a industrial chemical plant explosion in the outskirts of the city — a disaster later determined to have been caused by deliberate negligence on the part of plant management, who had falsified safety records for years. The explosion killed thirty-one workers. Roberto arrived in the second wave, when the fires had been partially contained but the site was still unstable, the air thick with particulate and the smell of burning synthetic material. His job was to document and collect physical evidence before the scene degraded further. He had worked disaster scenes before. He told himself this was no different.

It was different. Midway through his documentation work, a secondary structural collapse occurred without warning. Roberto was thrown to the ground by the concussive force. When he looked up, two colleagues were buried under debris less than twenty feet away. He was uninjured. They were not. He spent the next forty minutes helping extract them before emergency crews arrived, his hands working mechanically while his mind registered details he could not stop registering — details that, as a forensic analyst, he was trained never to look away from. Both colleagues survived, though one lost a hand. Roberto finished his shift.

He did not tell Marisol what had happened until three weeks later, when she found him sitting in the kitchen at 2 a.m., unable to explain why.

Sleep has become unreliable territory. Roberto lies down each night beside his wife and waits, knowing that at some point the images will come — not as dreams exactly, but as a kind of involuntary replay that feels more like reliving than remembering. The smell is always part of it. At work, certain chemical compounds used in evidence processing can trigger it without warning. He has learned to identify which ones and to leave the room before the sensation fully takes hold, offering his younger colleagues technical explanations for why he is stepping out. He has become skilled at this kind of quiet management.

What troubles him more than the nights is what has happened to his concentration. Roberto built his professional identity on precision, on the ability to hold complex information in careful order. Now he finds himself re-reading the same paragraph of a lab report, losing the thread of his own analysis mid-sentence. He has begun double-checking his work in ways he never needed to before, arriving early to review documentation he completed the day before, afraid of errors he cannot afford to make. He has not told his supervisor.

At home, Roberto is present in the way that a man can be present without quite being there. He and Marisol have dinner together most evenings. He asks about her day. He is not unkind. But there is a distance she has named and he has not disputed — a kind of glass wall that went up after the explosion and has not come down. On weekends he tends the small garden behind their house with a focus that Marisol recognizes as something other than enjoyment. He is managing himself, she says. He agrees, though he would not have used that word six months ago.

What Roberto returns to most often, in the quiet moments he cannot fill with work or routine, is a question that has no forensic answer: he was the one standing in the right place. His colleagues were in the wrong place. There was no variable he could have measured that would have predicted it. For a man whose life's work depends on evidence leading somewhere, this remains the most destabilizing fact of all.
